source.version: Journal version of record: Science Advances 10, eadn5290 (2024), published 12 July 2024 (submitted 14 December 2023, accepted 7 June 2024). Main article only; the Supplementary Materials (sections S1 to S9, tables S1 to S18, figs. S1 to S6) are not in this PDF.
source.title_on_document: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content

paper_design_summary: In a preregistered online experiment on Prolific (UK), 293 writers wrote an eight-sentence short story after random assignment to Human-only, Human with one GenAI idea (option to request one three-sentence GPT-4 story idea), or Human with five GenAI ideas (option to request up to five). A separate group of 600 Prolific evaluators, blind to condition, rated six randomly assigned stories each on novelty, usefulness, and emotional characteristics (3519 evaluations). The authors also computed embedding-based similarity of each story to the other stories in its condition and to the GenAI idea.

studies.label: Writer experiment (short-story writing with optional GPT-4 story ideas), rated by a separate evaluator sample

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writer condition: Human-only (no mention of or access to generative AI), Human with one GenAI idea (option to request one GPT-4 story idea), or Human with five GenAI ideas (option to request up to five). Topic (open seas, jungle, different planet) was also randomized. Analysis is intention-to-treat by assigned condition.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomized into one of three experimental conditions: Human-only, Human with one GenAI idea, and Human with five GenAI ideas.
assignment.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, Writer study and experimental conditions; also p. 2, Fig. 1 caption
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 8, Preregistration and ethics approval: AsPredicted.org (ID 136723); copy in section S9 (not in this PDF)

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Writers wrote the story with no mention of or access to generative AI. Three writers in this arm who admitted using generative AI were dropped per the preregistration.

arms.name: Human with one GenAI idea
arms.description: Option to click 'Generate Story Idea' once and receive a three-sentence story idea from GPT-4; 82 of 100 writers requested it.

arms.name: Human with five GenAI ideas
arms.description: Option to request up to five three-sentence GPT-4 story ideas; 93 of 98 writers requested at least one, 2.55 on average, 24.5 percent requested all five.

participants.exclusions: 500 Prolific participants began the writer study; 169 exited before giving consent, 22 were dropped for not giving consent, 13 dropped out before completing, and 3 Human-only writers who admitted using generative AI were dropped per the preregistration, leaving 293 writers and 293 stories. The number randomized is not stated (randomization followed consent and the DAT; it is not stated whether the 13 dropouts left before or after assignment). DAT score was computed for 291 of 293 writers. Ratings came from a separate sample of 600 evaluators (3519 evaluations); evaluators were not assigned to AI.
participants.who: Prolific participants based in the United Kingdom with approval rating of at least 95 percent from 100 to 1,000,000 prior submissions, not selected on writing skill or creativity (writers). Evaluators were a separate Prolific UK sample that had not taken part in the writer study.
participants.quote: Three participants in the Human-only condition admitted to using generative AI during their story writing exercise and—as per our preregistration—were therefore dropped from the analysis, resulting in a total number of writers and stories of 293.
participants.locator: p. 7, Materials and Methods, Writer study and experimental conditions; arm counts p. 2, Results, Baseline versus generative AI conditions

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 via the GPT API
ai_tool.how_used: On request, the interface sent the prompt 'Write a three-sentence summary of a story about [topic]' to GPT-4 and showed the writer the three-sentence idea. Writers could not copy and paste the idea, could not customize the prompt, and could not interact with the model repeatedly (p. 6, p. 7).

task.description: Write a short story of exactly eight sentences, in English, appropriate for a teenage and young adult audience (about 15 to 24 years), on a randomly assigned topic: an adventure on the open seas, in the jungle, or on a different planet. Writers first completed the Divergent Association Task (DAT).

outcomes.name: Novelty index (evaluator-rated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average of three 9-point items rated by blind Prolific evaluators: novel, original, rare (Cronbach alpha 0.92). Preregistered index. Results qualitatively unchanged with evaluator, story-order, and topic fixed effects and an indicator for accessing at least one AI idea (table S4, not in this PDF). Components shown in Fig. 2A.

contrasts.reported: increase of 5.4% (b = 0.207, P = 0.021, see table S3); OLS coefficient with P printed, SE not in the main text; Fig. 2A plots the coefficient with an interval
contrasts.locator: p. 3, Results (text continuing from p. 2); Fig. 2A, p. 3

contrasts.reported: increase in novelty of 8.1% (b = 0.311, P < 0.001)
contrasts.locator: p. 3, Results; Fig. 2A, p. 3

outcomes.name: Usefulness index (evaluator-rated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average of three 9-point items rated by blind evaluators: appropriate, feasible, publishable (Cronbach alpha 0.89); usefulness adapted to mean appropriateness for the audience, feasibility of developing into a complete book, and likelihood a publisher would develop it. Preregistered index. Robust to the fixed effects in table S4 (not in this PDF).

contrasts.locator: p. 3, Results; Fig. 2A, p. 3

contrasts.locator: p. 3, Results; Fig. 2A, p. 3

outcomes.name: Similarity of story to other stories in the same condition (embedding)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity (x100, range 0 to 100) between the embedding of the focal story and the average embedding of all other stories in the same condition. Higher similarity means lower diversity, so the sign is reversed relative to diversity. In the Human-only condition similarity scores span 8.10 points; the authors express the increases as 10.7 and 8.9 percent of that range. Fig. 4A shows kernel densities by condition.

contrasts.reported: Similarity higher in treatment, so diversity lower (sign reversed): b = 0.871, P < 0.001, see table S11; 10.7% of the 8.10-point Human-only range
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Results, Similarity of stories; Fig. 4, p. 5

contrasts.reported: Similarity higher in treatment, so diversity lower (sign reversed): b = 0.718, P = 0.003; 8.9% of the 8.10-point Human-only range
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Results, Similarity of stories; Fig. 4, p. 5

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity x 100 of each story's embedding to the average embedding of all other stories in its condition
diversity_detail.embedding_model: OpenAI embeddings API (specific model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each output against the centroid of all other outputs in its condition (leave-one-out centroid)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS on story-level similarity scores with condition dummies, robust standard errors (writer-study outcomes: one story per writer); p. 8, Statistical analysis
diversity_detail.notes: Paper reports similarity, not diversity; a positive coefficient means more homogeneous stories. Table S11 not in this PDF.

company_involvement.description: Funding from the University of Exeter Business School and UCL School of Management; authors declare no competing interests. GPT-4 was used through OpenAI's API, with no stated OpenAI involvement.

eligibility.reason: Writers were randomized to no AI or to the option of receiving one or up to five GPT-4 story ideas (p. 7); 293 writers analyzed (p. 7), 100 and 98 in the two AI arms (p. 2); stories were rated for novelty and usefulness by blind evaluators and scored for embedding similarity (pp. 3-5). AI arms offer the idea as an option (88.4 percent took it); estimates are intention-to-treat.

one_line_finding: Access to up to five GPT-4 story ideas raised evaluator-rated novelty by 8.1 percent (b = 0.311, P < 0.001) and usefulness by 9.0 percent (b = 0.453, P < 0.001), and raised each story's similarity to other stories in its condition (one idea b = 0.871, P < 0.001; five ideas b = 0.718, P = 0.003) (pp. 3-4, Figs. 2 and 4).
open_questions: Human-only arm size is not printed; 293 minus 100 minus 98 gives 95, left null because the paper does not state it.
Number randomized is not stated: it is unclear whether the 13 writers who dropped out before completing had already been assigned.

Main text prints only coefficients and P values; SEs and arm means are in supplementary tables S3, S6, and S11, which are not in this PDF. The pooled AI-versus-Human-only preregistered test is in section S4, also not in this PDF.
Codebook rule 3 (arm closest to free chatbot use) does not separate the two AI arms, since both supply ideas; the primary record must pick one.
Construct coding of the exploratory items (well written, twist, changed expectations) is a judgment call between usefulness/novelty and other.
notes: Supplementary Materials (sections S1 to S9, tables S1 to S18, figs. S1 to S6) are referenced but not included in the PDF. Evaluator-rated outcomes are regressions at the evaluation level (3519 evaluations of 293 stories by 600 evaluators) with SEs clustered by evaluator (p. 8); clustering is not by writer, the unit of assignment. Story similarity outcomes are writer-level OLS with robust SEs. Heterogeneity by DAT (pre-treatment creativity, mean 77.24, SD 6.48, n = 291): among low-DAT writers, one and five ideas raise novelty by 6.3 and 10.7 percent and usefulness by 5.5 and 11.5 percent; five ideas raise well written by up to 26.6 percent and enjoyment by up to 22.6 percent and cut boring by up to 15.2 percent; little effect for high-DAT writers (p. 4, Fig. 3; tables S9 and S10 not in PDF). Not listed as outcomes: evaluator judgments of whether a story was written by AI, ownership and profit-split ratings after disclosure (ownership penalty of at least 25 percent, p. 6), and ethics attitudes; these are perception measures (section S5). Writer DAT is a pre-treatment covariate, not an outcome.
